title: BERA Continues to Publish Articles with Fake References
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Stephen Vainker documents that BERA published two additional journal articles containing fake AI-generated references within two weeks of issuing what he calls a 'ludicrously triumphant retraction statement,' bringing its total count of affected papers to 21. The new publications span the Curriculum Journal and the British Journal of Educational Technology, with specific fabricated citations identified and documented in each. Vainker argues that BERA is trapped in an untenable position: simultaneously issuing retractions while attacking the whistleblower's methods as 'unsound and ethically problematic' and falsely claiming credit for retractions it was publicly prompted to make. He contends that this posture leaves the organisation no credible retreat position as educational scrutiny of its journals intensifies. The article characterises BERA's ongoing complacency as a symptom of misplaced institutional confidence — the assumption that established reputation can outlast mounting documentary evidence of editorial failure across four journals.
points: Within two weeks of issuing its retraction statement, BERA published two more papers with fake AI-generated references, demonstrating that the editorial failure is not historical but ongoing and unresolved at the journal management level.

BERA's strategy of claiming credit for whistleblower-prompted retractions, misrepresenting COPE guidelines, and attacking the complainant's methodology leaves it with no defensible position when scrutiny intensifies — it cannot later claim lessons were learned from a process it publicly declared was conducted correctly.

The total of 21 papers with fake or impossible references across four journals points to a systemic editorial weakness, not isolated incidents — a pattern that individual retractions cannot address without structural reform of review processes.
quotes: BERA is getting itself into an awful mess. Two weeks ago, it began the process of retracting papers following my discovery of many, many AI-authored papers in its four journals.

These two retractions now indicate that, even after 19 retractions, leadership across BERA journals is incapable of stemming the tide of AI dreck being published in its journals. BERA, sooner or later, will need to face up to the fact that there have been serious editorial failures across its four journals.

BERA is trying to issue retractions while insisting that it is in the right and I am in the wrong. That is a completely absurd position that rests on falsely claiming credit for discovering things I publicly informed them of, misrepresenting COPE guidelines, and claiming, completely baselessly, that my methods are 'unsound and ethically problematic.'
All of these things are easy to disprove. BERA will have to adopt a more self-critical, and therefore defensible, position.

BERA seems to think that because it is such a well-established and well-supported organisation, it can simply ride out my criticisms without taking them seriously. As with John Hattie, the problem they face is that I am right.

Before long, BERA will not be able to avoid scrutiny, and their weirdly triumphant current response will mean that they will have no position to retreat to. They will not be able to say lessons were learned if in response to beginning retractions they brazenly took the moral high ground while continuing to publish AI dreck.
BERA doesn't realise it, but it is running out of time to save its reputation, and its remarkable (in the circumstances) complacency does not inspire confidence.
